rv.q: Here’s the wry humour and secret misery; the sense of a society boring itself to death. But this is in fact Turgenev, writing more than 40 years before The Seagull’s premiere in 1896, and already trialling the deeply perceptive, subtext-driven drama that Chekhov would perfect.
Leading Lyndsey Turner’s consummately acted Donmar revival of A Month in the Country, Sophie Okonedo is mesmerising as the bored, married Natalya Petrovna.
It’s great fun: sheer proximity to the actors at the Donmar makes it feel as if we’re spying on them from a thicket.
Now add Brian Friel, whose sparkling script “after Turgenev” is spun so delicately that it appears both of its time and a universal story of pained love and marriage.
Here, Turner prunes it into a witty, approachable form – but leaves all its thorns intact.

Director Lyndsey Turner handles the piece skilfully, allowing events to unfold at a rhythm just slow enough to drive home the stiflingly dull state of the characters’ lives without becoming tedious, and with enough crackling tension and humour to remain utterly engaging.
There’s a constant undercurrent of humour in Lyndsey Turner’s production at the Donmar Warehouse.
Sadly, Turner’s production wobbles uncertainly between both scenarios, ungoverned by a leading lady’s controlling hand.
It’s a gloriously rich play, wonderfully realised in a production that holds its contradictions gently in its hands and just lets its subtleties reveal themselves.
The result is a quiet, witty, and gently entertaining piece of theatre that leisurely examines the volatile passions of the upperclass.
The result is a thoroughly engrossing and deeply enjoyable production that delivers all the emotional complexity of a Russian classic while remaining wonderfully entertaining throughout.
Lyndsey Turner's production of Turgenev's comedy, A Month in the Country, has real charm.
Okonedo’s snippy-snappy handling of dialogue and on-a-dime mood swings are razor-sharp, and she and the rest of the uniformly fine cast land this well oiled comedy impressively.
Ms Okonedo most assuredly delivers the goods in this production.
Okonedo, unfortunately, doesn’t seem quite right for the role; she has too much natural gravitas, and the coquettishness feels forced.
The best Month in the Country I have seen is Frederick Ashton’s fifty-minute succinct ballet, which extracted the essence and heightened emotion without the tedium.
It is her electrical personality which will dominate the next two and a half wickedly enjoyable hours in old Russia.

A Month in the Country is a brilliant play that transcends eras and despite the original being over 150 years old, and Friel’s being over three decades in age it feels as contemporary and original today.
A Month in the Country is a bitter-sweet exploration of heart over head and a delight from start to finish.

A smart revival, this play pulls audiences into moments of familiarity and farce, while evoking a much deeper question of whether the lives these characters have built can ever satisfy what they truly want.
Okonedo's performance here takes it to the next level.

cn.t: Turner's production of Friel's Turgenev adaptation earns strong praise for Okonedo's captivating performance and witty direction, though some critics find the claustrophobic staging constrains the action and the tonal balance uneven.
